title: The third council
hookLine: the Theravada chronicles place a council at Pataliputta under Ashoka

cards: In a monastery in the capital, the monks have stopped meeting. On the observance days, when they should gather to recite the rules together, they stay apart, because they no longer trust who among them is really a monk.
The chronicles of Sri Lanka say outsiders had put on robes for the food and the honor, and brought their own teachings with them. The king sends a minister to set things right.
In the chronicle's telling, it goes badly wrong.

teach.b: First, the order gone wrong. The minister, the Mahavamsa says, misunderstands his instructions.

When the monks still refuse to hold the observance with the others, he draws his sword and kills some of them, until the king's own brother, a monk, steps in front of the blade. Ashoka is horrified: is the guilt mine?
The king sends for a senior monk, Moggaliputta Tissa, who tells him that without the intention, there is no guilt in the deed.
Elsewhere the Buddha says it is intention he calls action; here that teaching meets a frightened king. Third, the question.
The elder and the king sit together, the chronicle says, and each monk is asked one thing: what did the Buddha teach?
Those who answer that he taught by analysis, taking things apart and looking, are kept; the others are sent away.
Then the community recites the teaching together, and the elder sets out a book that answers wrong views point by point. Fourth, whose memory this is.
This council is told in the Theravada chronicles kept in Sri Lanka, the Dipavamsa and the Mahavamsa. Other Buddhist schools tell Ashoka's time differently, and some place councils elsewhere.
That isn't a scandal; every family remembers its own story.
So today's line is careful: not that it happened just so, but that the chronicles remember.
And it matters to the Theravada world, because the chronicle goes on to tell of teachers sent out from that council to other lands. Tomorrow, one of them crosses the sea.

how: In Theravada countries the council at Pataliputta is counted among the great councils that preserved the teaching, and the elder Moggaliputta Tissa is remembered as its leader.

games.q: you're the king. your minister has killed monks while carrying out your order, which he misunderstood. what do you do?
o: ask a wise elder whether the guilt is yours.
games.why: Ashoka sends for Moggaliputta Tissa, who answers that without intention there is no guilt, and then helps him purify the community.

practice: Your tradition might be a faith, a family, a culture, or simply the way you were raised to see the world.

Find one question about it you've never asked, where a custom came from, who first taught your family a prayer or a recipe, who tells the story differently, and hold it for a few breaths without answering.
Then think where you might look, or whom you might ask.

wordCard.voice: Moggaliputta Tissa. The elder who told Ashoka that without intention there is no guilt, then asked each monk what the Buddha taught.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit: sangiti, the word for these councils, a reciting together.

carryVoice: Your line: the chronicles remember. Every community keeps its own memory of its past. Until tomorrow.
